name: Revenue Equivalence
plain_language_definition: Different auction rules can produce the same expected seller revenue under specific assumptions.
everyday_problem: The problem is comparing auction formats that look different: first-price, second-price, English, and others may create different bidding behavior.
first_principles_reason: Revenue equivalence exists because different rules can sometimes generate the same expected payment once bidders adjust their strategies.
mathematical_principle: Truthful behavior must give at least as much payoff as each profitable lie. The useful relation is `u_i(truth) >= u_i(report) for every alternative report.`. In plain language: The inequality says a person should not gain by replacing the truthful action with another report.
why_it_matters: This concept matters because it turns a loose strategic story into a checkable claim about what someone would actually choose. The theorem teaches which differences are cosmetic and which assumptions do real work.
what_breaks_without_it: Without this concept, the analysis can name the players and choices but cannot tell whether the proposed behavior survives individual incentives. This is a theorem about a family of environments, not a universal slogan. Its usefulness is that it tells you exactly which assumptions make format differences wash out.
naive_problem: The naive move is to describe what happened and call it rational. The course asks for more: what choice problem made that behavior sensible from the player's own point of view?
failed_simple_approach: The simple story fails when another feasible action, another belief, or another continuation would make the player want to do something else.
mathematical_object: The object is a theorem linking allocation rules and expected payments under assumptions such as risk neutrality, independent private values, and symmetric bidders.
operation: Check whether the auction gives the object to the same type of bidder and gives the lowest type the same expected payoff; then expected revenue can coincide.
worked_mini_example: First-price and second-price auctions induce different bids, but under the theorem's assumptions the seller's expected revenue can match because bidders strategically shade in one format and bid truthfully in another.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture treats this as a working instrument for reading examples, payoff tables, game trees, and applications, not as a term to memorize. The lecture placement matters: this concept is introduced exactly where the previous representation would otherwise stop explaining the example.
common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to quote revenue equivalence without the assumptions. Change risk, affiliation, reserve prices, or asymmetry and the result can fail.
cross_course_connections: The same primitive returns whenever the course asks whether a proposed behavior is compatible with incentives, beliefs, timing, or information. The theorem matters because it separates surface format from deeper allocation and incentive structure. Two auctions can look different to bidders yet be equivalent for expected seller revenue under strict assumptions.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for auction comparisons where allocation sameness and bidder payoff normalization drive payment conclusions.

name: Ad Auctions
plain_language_definition: Auction design applied to online ad slots where position, clicks, and value interact.
everyday_problem: The problem is selling attention slots, not a single physical object. Position affects clicks, quality affects usefulness, and bids interact with platform rules.
first_principles_reason: Ad auctions exist because online markets must allocate ranked slots repeatedly and automatically while advertisers have private values per click.
mathematical_principle: Truthful behavior must give at least as much payoff as each profitable lie. The useful relation is `u_i(truth) >= u_i(report) for every alternative report.`. In plain language: The inequality says a person should not gain by replacing the truthful action with another report.
why_it_matters: This concept matters because it turns a loose strategic story into a checkable claim about what someone would actually choose. That mix makes the auction a live system-design problem, not only a classroom bidding game.
what_breaks_without_it: Without this concept, the analysis can name the players and choices but cannot tell whether the proposed behavior survives individual incentives. The online setting also introduces repeated participation and measurement. Clicks are both the object being priced and a noisy signal about match quality.
naive_problem: The naive move is to describe what happened and call it rational. The course asks for more: what choice problem made that behavior sensible from the player's own point of view?
failed_simple_approach: The simple story fails when another feasible action, another belief, or another continuation would make the player want to do something else.
mathematical_object: The object is a sponsored-search mechanism combining bids, click-through rates, quality scores, allocation order, and per-click payments.
operation: Rank advertisers by the platform's scoring rule, assign slots, then compute payments from the rule that determines what each advertiser must pay per click.
worked_mini_example: A lower bidder with a highly relevant ad may beat a higher bidder if quality affects ranking. The mechanism is not just who writes the biggest number.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture treats this as a working instrument for reading examples, payoff tables, game trees, and applications, not as a term to memorize. The lecture placement matters: this concept is introduced exactly where the previous representation would otherwise stop explaining the example.

Ad auctions add engineering detail to mechanism design. The platform is not merely selling an item; it is ranking ads, pricing clicks, and balancing advertiser value with user relevance.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for markets with ranked slots, click probabilities, quality scores, and generalized second-price style rules.

name: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium
plain_language_definition: An equilibrium for dynamic games with beliefs that stay consistent with observed behavior.
everyday_problem: The problem is dynamic play with hidden information: after observing actions, players must update beliefs and continue choosing rationally.
first_principles_reason: PBE exists because dynamic Bayesian games need both credible continuation behavior and believable beliefs about what has happened.
mathematical_principle: A belief is a probability distribution over states, types, or histories. The useful relation is `E[u(a, theta)] = sum_theta p(theta) u(a, theta).`. In plain language: theta is the unknown type or state; p(theta) is its probability; expected utility averages payoffs across possibilities.
why_it_matters: This concept matters because it turns a loose strategic story into a checkable claim about what someone would actually choose.
what_breaks_without_it: Without this concept, the analysis can name the players and choices but cannot tell whether the proposed behavior survives individual incentives. The hard part is off-path beliefs. When an unexpected signal appears, Bayes' rule may not pin down beliefs, so the model must still specify beliefs carefully.
naive_problem: The naive move is to describe what happened and call it rational. The course asks for more: what choice problem made that behavior sensible from the player's own point of view?
failed_simple_approach: The simple story fails when another feasible action, another belief, or another continuation would make the player want to do something else.
mathematical_object: The object is a strategy profile plus a belief system, with sequential rationality and belief consistency where Bayes' rule applies.
operation: At each information set, check that the strategy is optimal given beliefs; then check that beliefs are updated consistently from the strategies whenever possible.
worked_mini_example: In a signaling game, seeing someone choose education may change an employer's belief about worker type. PBE checks both the education choice and the employer's updated response.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture treats this as a working instrument for reading examples, payoff tables, game trees, and applications, not as a term to memorize. The lecture placement matters: this concept is introduced exactly where the previous representation would otherwise stop explaining the example. That is why PBE belongs after signaling and Bayesian games: it combines dynamic credibility with disciplined belief updating.
common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to focus only on strategies and forget beliefs. In hidden-information dynamic games, beliefs are part of the equilibrium object.
cross_course_connections: The same primitive returns whenever the course asks whether a proposed behavior is compatible with incentives, beliefs, timing, or information. PBE is where beliefs become part of credibility. A continuation action is not enough; the model must also say what the player believes after seeing a history or signal.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for dynamic asymmetric-information models with off-path beliefs, updating, and sequential rationality.

name: Signaling
plain_language_definition: Using an action or message to convey private information when others update beliefs from it.
everyday_problem: The problem is how someone with private information can convince others of it through an observable action.
first_principles_reason: Signaling exists because words or actions can change beliefs only if different types have different incentives or costs.
mathematical_principle: A belief is a probability distribution over states, types, or histories. The useful relation is `E[u(a, theta)] = sum_theta p(theta) u(a, theta).`. In plain language: theta is the unknown type or state; p(theta) is its probability; expected utility averages payoffs across possibilities.
why_it_matters: This concept matters because it turns a loose strategic story into a checkable claim about what someone would actually choose. The receiver's belief update is therefore just as important as the sender's action.
what_breaks_without_it: Without this concept, the analysis can name the players and choices but cannot tell whether the proposed behavior survives individual incentives. Separating and pooling are the two core patterns. In separating equilibria, different types choose different signals; in pooling equilibria, signals fail to distinguish types.
naive_problem: The naive move is to describe what happened and call it rational. The course asks for more: what choice problem made that behavior sensible from the player's own point of view?
failed_simple_approach: The simple story fails when another feasible action, another belief, or another continuation would make the player want to do something else.
mathematical_object: The object is a sender-receiver game with types, signals, receiver beliefs, and receiver actions.
operation: For each possible type, compare the payoff from sending each signal; then check how the receiver updates beliefs and responds.
worked_mini_example: Education can signal worker ability if high-ability workers find education less costly. The diploma matters not because it directly produces all value, but because it separates types under the right incentives.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture treats this as a working instrument for reading examples, payoff tables, game trees, and applications, not as a term to memorize. The lecture placement matters: this concept is introduced exactly where the previous representation would otherwise stop explaining the example.
common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to assume any costly action is a signal. It signals only if costs and incentives differ across types in a way receivers can reason from.
cross_course_connections: The same primitive returns whenever the course asks whether a proposed behavior is compatible with incentives, beliefs, timing, or information. Signaling is costly communication through action. The central question is why a low type would not imitate a high type, and the answer must come from different costs or benefits across types.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for actions that are valuable mainly because observers infer hidden quality, commitment, or type from them.

name: Cheap Talk
plain_language_definition: Costless messages that matter only when incentives make them credible enough to influence beliefs.
everyday_problem: The problem is whether costless messages can influence behavior when the speaker may want to mislead.
first_principles_reason: Cheap talk exists because communication has no direct cost or binding force, so credibility must come from aligned incentives rather than from the message itself.
mathematical_principle: A belief is a probability distribution over states, types, or histories. The useful relation is `E[u(a, theta)] = sum_theta p(theta) u(a, theta).`. In plain language: theta is the unknown type or state; p(theta) is its probability; expected utility averages payoffs across possibilities.
why_it_matters: This concept matters because it turns a loose strategic story into a checkable claim about what someone would actually choose. The lecture point is that speech can be strategic even when it is free.
what_breaks_without_it: Without this concept, the analysis can name the players and choices but cannot tell whether the proposed behavior survives individual incentives. The interesting case is partial alignment. If interests are perfectly opposed, talk often collapses; if they are close enough, messages can partition information usefully.
naive_problem: The naive move is to describe what happened and call it rational. The course asks for more: what choice problem made that behavior sensible from the player's own point of view?
failed_simple_approach: The simple story fails when another feasible action, another belief, or another continuation would make the player want to do something else.
mathematical_object: The object is a sender-receiver game where messages do not directly change payoffs but can change beliefs and actions.
operation: Compare what each type of sender wants the receiver to do. If interests are aligned enough, informative messages can be credible; if not, messages may pool and reveal little.
worked_mini_example: A restaurant reviewer saying this is good may be useful if their incentives match yours. A seller saying trust me may not be informative if every seller would say it.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture treats this as a working instrument for reading examples, payoff tables, game trees, and applications, not as a term to memorize. The lecture placement matters: this concept is introduced exactly where the previous representation would otherwise stop explaining the example.
common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to say cheap means irrelevant. Costless speech can matter when incentives make truthful communication self-enforcing.
cross_course_connections: The same primitive returns whenever the course asks whether a proposed behavior is compatible with incentives, beliefs, timing, or information. Cheap talk is the opposite stress test from signaling: if messages cost nothing and bind no one, only aligned incentives can make them informative. The message works when lying would not help enough.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for models where messages are nonbinding and the key question is whether incentives allow information transmission.

name: Common Knowledge
plain_language_definition: A fact that everyone knows, everyone knows everyone knows, and so on.
everyday_problem: The problem is that coordinated action may require more than everyone privately knowing a fact. People may also need to know that others know it, and know that others know that others know it.
first_principles_reason: Common knowledge exists because higher-order uncertainty can block coordination. A public fact can support behavior that a private fact cannot.
mathematical_principle: Common knowledge means everyone knows, everyone knows everyone knows, and the chain continues. The useful relation is `E, KE, KKE, KKKE, ...`. In plain language: E is the event; K means known by the players; repeated K's represent higher-order knowledge.
why_it_matters: This concept matters because it turns a loose strategic story into a checkable claim about what someone would actually choose.
what_breaks_without_it: Without this concept, the analysis can name the players and choices but cannot tell whether the proposed behavior survives individual incentives. The infinite chain sounds abstract, but it explains concrete coordination. Public announcements, market conventions, and shared rules work partly because each person can rely on others having the same public reference point.
naive_problem: The naive move is to describe what happened and call it rational. The course asks for more: what choice problem made that behavior sensible from the player's own point of view?
failed_simple_approach: The simple story fails when another feasible action, another belief, or another continuation would make the player want to do something else.
mathematical_object: The object is an infinite hierarchy: the event is known, everyone knows it is known, everyone knows everyone knows it is known, and so on.
operation: Start with the event, then ask whether each level of mutual awareness is satisfied. Common knowledge requires the chain not to stop at a finite level.
worked_mini_example: If a policy change is announced publicly, firms may coordinate on the new rule. If each firm only hears it privately and doubts whether others heard it, behavior may not shift the same way.
lecture_emphasis: The lecture treats this as a working instrument for reading examples, payoff tables, game trees, and applications, not as a term to memorize. The lecture placement matters: this concept is introduced exactly where the previous representation would otherwise stop explaining the example.
common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to treat true, known, and common knowledge as the same. They are different levels of shared awareness.
cross_course_connections: The same primitive returns whenever the course asks whether a proposed behavior is compatible with incentives, beliefs, timing, or information. Common knowledge explains why publicness can matter as much as truth. A fact can be true and individually known, yet fail to coordinate behavior if people doubt whether others know that they know.
recognize_in_new_work: Look for coordination failures, public announcements, or arguments that depend on what everyone knows about everyone else's knowledge.
